scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Calinda emerged in the 1720s from African combat dances, specifically linked to the Kingdom of Kongo.
It spread through the French colonial Caribbean and to Louisiana, where it became a central part of Afro-Caribbean cultural expression.
It was used by enslaved people for entertainment and, in Haiti, as a tactical preparation for armed conflict.
on_screen: Map: Caribbean (Trinidad and Tobago, Haiti, Guadeloupe, Martinique), United States (Louisiana) · Caribbean

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Calinda is performed during Carnival in Trinidad and Guadeloupe.
In Haiti, it is associated with Voodoo ceremonies and festivals.
It serves as a martial art, a war dance, and a form of social entertainment that preserves African cultural identity.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed as a ritualized stick-fight.
In Trinidad, fighters enter a gayelle to compete.
In some historical Haitian versions, dancers jumped over water bottles while brandishing sticks.
Watch for Stick-fighting.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music is central to the practice, featuring call-and-response chants called lavways.
Instruments include primitive drums beaten with hands, banjos, and 'the quills' (pipes bound together).
Listen for the drums, banjos, the quills, triangles.
The music is driven by rapid hand-beaten drums, including a large four-foot drum played by two men, accompanied by banjos and quills, creating a whirling, tumultuous sound.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: In Trinidad, stick-fighters perform in a gayelle.
Historically, in New Orleans, the dance took place in public squares like Place Congo.
Costumes vary; in some historical contexts, performers wore specific attire, and in theatrical representations, court costumes were used as prizes.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Variants include l'agya, damaye, and mayolé in Guadeloupe and Martinique; Ladja baton in Martinique; and stick-licking or stick science in Barbados.
The dance is related to Capoeira, Juego de maní, and Bamboula.
